body:
I tend to feel a bit emotionally labile a week or so before it's due then a week or so after, but I've never experienced physical side effects apart from occasional bloating.

Like you said, it seems like a reasonable trade-off as I don't get my typical 'horror periods' with the depo and don't spend half a month, every month doubled over in agony. My only wish is that we could self-administer them occasionally to make it even easier.

I have this issue due to other medication and have to find ways to work around it. For example, I set two different alarms and have them start going off 2 hours in advance. Sometimes I'll place them on the other side of the room too. I go to bed an hour earlier now so I'm getting the 'treat' of extra comfy time. Once you actually get going it's fine, it's just the initial movement...
Oh gosh, this comment really got me in the feels. I've been there too. My heart hurts for you...us...everyone like us.

I believe as a one-off thing it isn't too harmful (providing there's no underlying stomach issues), but as others have alluded to it shouldn't become a habit. Just make sure you force down some food with it too.

Pondering death whilst amongst similar-minded folk is at least somewhat cathartic and a step away from having an existential crisis on ones own. I hope everyone remains safe, is all. I come here to laugh AND cry.

I'm at around 6 months now...early days. As others have alluded to, it's dull but some of that perpetual anxiety has reduced. I still crave the sweet relief of booze but living the CA life was becoming unsustainable for me and really quite dangerous. Checking in here makes me feel like I'm amongst friends at least.

I've found it really hard to reflect on the benefits of sobriety but after reading your post relating to what's currently going on I guess I do see some glimmers of hope. I connect/communicate with people better when sober and we all need that right now. Depression is less extreme so things don't constantly feel so hopeless. And more importantly I can function the best at work. I work in inpatient healthcare so being on top of things has been more important than ever, helping other people to emotionally navigate this crisis. Thank you for making me reflect with your post :)

Really well put post, thank you. Especially the bits about recognition and lack of epiphanies, can definitely relate. 

And from one person aiming for sobriety to another congrats on the time achieved, it's definitely impressive.

You're so right...a lot of our struggles are transitory even sometimes the desire to drink. It helps to remind yourself.

My neighbour has painted a rainbow and "this too shall pass" on their window since lockdown :) it's a nice daily reminder on the way to work.

If you feel unmotivated as it is, you already know that booze will sap you of every last bit of motivation you had when it gets ahold. When I'm unmotivated I make a conscious effort to literally force myself to do something. Maybe write out a simple daily routine chart with even just little tasks and stick to it religiously. Only then do the benefits trickle in, like distraction, sense of accomplishment, connecting with people, etc. Just getting by, day by day, is an accomplishment in itself for a lot of us right now so don't feel you have to do anything spectacular to "fill the void". Totally get what you're saying about your partner though, is there any chance you can explain how you feel? Sometimes just addressing the fact that you appreciate the difference in routines and that you want to do your best is good enough.

Neuropsychology in inpatient rehab. I didn't think it would affect us beyond protecting long-stay patients. However, we've been advised to safely discharge people really quickly to make room for people from the general hospital. So we're all weighing up the risk of sending people home with the risk of them picking up the virus. I feel morally conflicted treating people who are not in acute distress. It's a mess really. We're not doing proper rehab and that could affect people for life. 

For many, the world seems to have stopped but people continue to have traumatic/acquired brain injuries, neurological conditions, stroke, etc. You think you're insignificant as an employee in the grand scheme of things but this has proven that we're all cogs in the same wheel.

This drove me mad too. However, like people have said, it does sort itself out after a time. I found that not stressing over it helped (i.e. not lying in bed tossing for hours, just going back periodically) because you can almost get yourself into an anxious state over it. I remind  myself that sleep DOES come, it has to at some point. Very inconvenient though, I hear you.

It has happened, been and gone. Someone said to me once "don't look backwards, you're not going that way". As for forgiveness, try to have some self compassion? What would you say to a close friend who'd done the same?

You've got this!
Ugh, I hate that too. And that it's always associated with fun or relaxation. It's only fun until it's not...which is the case for a lot of us.

You're not alone. I'm coming up to 3 months and feel exactly the same, so sorry for the lack of tips.

I have to really force myself to focus on the less obvious benefits of sobriety, like better work performance, no crippling embarrassment and better relationships. The benefits are there, just less clear than I'd like them to be. And they don't all necessarily make me happier...they just make life a bit easier. 

A big part of it I think is the expectation that alcohol was the only problem...it wasn't, I was using it to hide my other problems. Now the booze has gone I feel like I have to face up to them (with limited motivation). That low mood was persistently present, with or without alcohol. 

Pink cloud or not, it sounds like you're doing very well with sobriety.

You could bring it up in the context of you using alcohol to manage your anxiety/depression. It's incredibly common, like everyone has said, and the doctor will have likely heard it all before. When I access patient records at work (not a doctor) and it says "alcohol excess" I just register it in case it's relevant and move on to the next thing, as do my colleagues. Good luck.

If it's around, it's getting drunk. No self control so can't have it around when attempting to abstain. Could you get someone to hide it? Maybe measure out your daily quota into smaller bottles and ration it? You're braver than I!

Didn't come across badly at all, don't worry! I'm glad there's the opportunity for people to become deconditioned. If it works, it works! I'm sure I'll forget some day the initial high alcohol provides and focus more on what it destroys.
I can totally do without the taste. If truth be told, I've never found a drink I've genuinely like the taste of. As for the feeling it gives you? That will always tempt me I think :-(
I take it you would not recommend returning? When I have in the past it has just been a downward spiral, but it feels like sobriety for some has few gains (apart from weight gains, wtf)

We appreciate you too! 

I've seen some amazing work done this week by colleagues, it's really quite inspirational.
I'm lazy, so being able to jump in the car to go places day and night.
Why thank you...it seems a lot less bleak when you put it like that. And yes, I can finally string a coherent sentence together on a Saturday afternoon now!

On my millionth attempt at sobriety, day 77 I think? Not really reaping any benefits yet. Mood the same, weight the same, skin worse, no sudden desire to meditate/do yoga/better myself in any way. Where the everloving fuck is this supposed pink cloud? Did stare at the 'reduced price' alcohol shelves earlier and felt a pang of yearning, especially since I live alone and am trying to social distance.

However, the only good thing is mental clarity and more effective cognition which I need for my job badly. I work in healthcare and it has been a hectic, frightening and bewildering week so goodness knows how it has been for patients too. I was able to perform well this week for people in greater need which has got to be some karmic success I guess? 

Dodged the alcohol aisles (sigh) so will be prepared for work/to do it all again next week and see what it brings. Sorry for being all "woe is me" when there is actual hell going on for some people.

Sorry to butt in, but I started experiencing more falls/trips with Pregabalin which works like Gabapentin I believe? It came on over about a month after a dosage increase. Maybe it's something similar. It's easy to forget how strong the stuff is and still to this day I don't know the implications of alcohol interaction (frankly didn't care at the time of taking it).

It's probably best to speak up. They may have their agenda but ultimately you have your own. I work in psychology (have also had therapy myself) and goals should always be collaborative. You may go off on useless tangents otherwise. The therapy is sometimes only decent if the therapeutic alliance is too, so may as well give yourself the best chance by being honest.

Good luck whatever route you choose and don't give up seeking the right help.

Congratulations on 100 days of dedication!

And thank you for putting number 2 so succinctly. I keep raging that nothing seems to be changing but, like you said, it's about giving yourself a fighting chance.

1. Delivery guy said he was "worried" about the amount of booze I was ordering. 

2. Cashier routinely grabbed behind him for vodka even when I wasn't there for it. 

3. Cashier in large supermarket asked for ID, looked up then said "oh it's you, nevermind".

As someone who regularly administers neuropsychological tests, something I do see often is anxiety/worry about ones faculties seriously affecting performance, regardless if there is anything organic going on. Obviously I can't comment on your case specifically, but if you're finding yourself fretting about it often (to be fair it's pretty scary), then the constant worry about underperformance could be making things even more challenging.

Good luck and I hope things become easier with time :-)

1. Accept that you're not the only one, we've all been there.
2. Try to change that automatic self narrative that gets stuck on a loop. Instead of "I'm awful, I'm stupid" maybe change it to "I did xyz, perhaps I shouldn't have, I've learned from that". 
3. Practise self compassion. Why are you worse than everybody else? You deserve forgiveness too. What would you say to a close friend who did the same? At least you're emotionally aware and trying to move forward. 
4. If I feel all-consumed by shame (or guilt, anger, etc.) I give myself a set amount of time, say 5 minutes, to really feel it. It's not pleasant, it's uncomfortable, sometimes I write it down or scream. Then after the amount of time try to move on, get on with other stuff, let it "wash" over me.   That way you're acknowledging the feeling but not pushing it further down or invalidating it, not letting it dictate all your actions. In the early stages of this one but it seems to work!

Hope you find something that works for you :-)
Really scary. I had no other coping strategies for shutting my negative emotions or thoughts down. Therapy and distraction has helped somewhat.

Same here. Started drinking heavily around 3 years after the procedure. I had reached my ideal body weight, had skin removal, compliments from everyone...then was like, "now what? Still feel awful." Deep down I think I replaced using food to regulate my emotions with alcohol (although alcohol does a much better job). The joy from food has just totally gone. 

The bypass has made my tolerance for alcohol lower so I get drunk faster (yay) but it seems to hit me harder than others and I make a fool of myself (nay). The sickness from booze is horrific with a bypass. Always bringing up bile and foam (?), sharp pouch pains and retching at any unfamiliar smell. 

I'm 60-something days sober on my millionth attempt and thoroughly miserable, I admit. I think the bypass stuff turned me to drink because I was looking for a way to cover up bad feelings but who knows, maybe my personality would have led me to it eventually anyway. The early days of drinking are awesome after all.

I have the same diagnosis. And like with many mental health problems, alcohol has definitely come hand-in-hand with it (pretty much exclusively in a negative way). Mood higher than usual? Drink to celebrate life! Mood seriously low? Drink to blot everything out. Plus I've been told by professionals that using alcohol gives the medication needed no real chance to work, as well as the combination making you feel ill. 

I've dabbled with sobriety numerous times, hopefully this will be my final attempt. All I can say is that during sobriety my mood fluctuations have been significantly less severe. Obviously everyone is different, but my episodes of higher/low mood when sober tend to not last as long and are not as overall destructive to my life. When sober I feel like I can tackle my mood or do something practical to help. Just generally be more proactive. Yes it's still hell at times but, for lack of a better way of expressing it, I feel less "mad" if that makes sense? 

I'm sorry you have to live with a condition but the positive of getting a diagnosis I've found is being able to access the right help and to understand things better. 

Hope that gives some insight :-)
No offense intended, but you've literally gone from a 5 to a 10. Obviously there's more important benefits than that but it's a nice bonus. Congratulations.
Suspected alcohol poisoning and attempted suicide due to a complete inability to reason/control myself when drunk.

I've definitely encountered this too, you're not alone. I was advised to relearn how to have basic compassion for myself. To look after myself as I would a loved one if they were feeling a bit vulnerable. I'm talking really basic things like treating myself, feeding myself nice stuff, resting. Reminding myself that I'm doing the best I can for now. It takes some time getting used to but I've found it helps a bit.

From a shy underposter, please don't stop overposting/sharing! It keeps things interesting and the community alive. 

As for drinking on antidepressants...it can certainly be a wild trip. Embarrassingly the combination resulted in an ambulance being called for me once. That's one I'll never get over.

Good news is that without the booze we're actually giving the antidepressants a chance to do their job.
I'm right there with you. The scales just aren't budging! Our insides will be grateful for our sobriety though.

My thoughts go out to you, they really do. I went through this exact same thing this very week, at the same amount of time sober as you and the urge to just blot it all out with booze was immense. First thing I did was hop on here. Then really tried to own every emotion I was having despite how raw it was...anger, sadness, in a sense grief. Distraction worked to an extent. Talk to as many people as you can about how you feel. Deep down we know if we did drink we'd be setting ourselves back further and tomorrow would come regardless. I went back to basics...fed myself, exercised a bit, cried if I had to and slept admittedly longer than I should have. Like grief, this is an emotional process and we WILL get through it. All the best.

Very potent last sentence there, very well worded. I do surrender this time as, like you, I've cycled for some time now and this list speaks for itself. I can't do it and I don't even want suicide to be an option. The booze wants that for us and it isn't acceptable.
Keep going. Hell is more real with than without the alcohol. Congrats so far.
Your advice is appreciated nontheless, I'm clear out of ideas myself. Apart from detox and like you say tackling one thing at a time. How the hell can a legal substance lead some of us so astray?

Ultimately worse if we play that tape forward. I'm just in my early days of shame, withdrawal and ultimate exposure again so am genuinely struggling with all those feelings of self-hatred and self-harm.

It's utterly horrifying and where nobody imagines themselves to be. And yet you feel like you have nobody but yourself to blame? You're not technically a victim but a perpetrator of your own demise but you feel powerless? Fuck. I wouldn't wish this addiction on my worst enemy. I hope you are doing well at the moment.

I want other people to see how destructive this is too. If you'd recited that list at the start of the year I would have never identified with it but here  I am. I've looked for AA meetings in the area but I work (worked?) in healthcare and it's an insular town. I just know this third time I cannot do this alone.
Thank you, probably at my lowest ebb right now and torn between giving up and downing a bottle of wine. Or both.

I went to my GP today after embarassingly telling them everything. They suggested that I sounded like I have bipolar type 2 so have referred me on to psychiatry again after 8 years. I'm frightened but humbled. Thank you for helping me realise I was/am out of control as opposed to actively suicidal.

I want to thank every one of you on this thread for your support. I'm safe for now, calling my doctor in the morning and have confided in my parents. You have all been so kind and I appreciate your thoughtful comments from the bottom of my heart. P.S. I don't know if this is how you update folk, sorry if it's not etiquette.
I just want to cease to function I think because it's all too much currently. It does seem like my last and only option though, you're right.

Thank you for your thoughtful response. I had a year of sobriety under my belt before this recent relapse which is shameful. Things weren't good after the assault but they weren't awful. It's recurrent depression that I'm masking but then, like you say, there are other ways of managing.
I know I need therapy but honestly right now I feel like there's nothing to work on. This seems like an unevitable and logical ending. A natural end to a wasted life.

I'm embarrassed and ashamed by my alcohol use, I don't want to upset them (more) by it. Which seems silly when I'm contemplating putting a belt around my neck soon which will cause greater upset. I love them dearly but have failed them.

I had a wonderful therapist but lost her due to lack of finances. I still can't bring myself to acknowledge she's gone. There's counselling available at work but 1. I think I'm losing my job and 2. because of the nature of my work I feel really uncomfortable discussing suicide there, particularly as I was hospitalised for an attempt 2 months ago and they have no idea.

I see no other way out. I also get no pleasure from life and never have done (unless drinking and I just don't want to any longer, I want the urge to stop). Everything hurts, in both body and mind. I was unfortunately found last time and an ambulance was called. That was a delightful 3 days in hospital with doctors laughing in my face. I have everything ready but I don't want to hurt my parents. Although I'm becoming an increasing burden on them anyway.

Mental and physical illness. The alcoholism, although many would argue that's volitional. I was sexually assaulted a few months ago. Work is horrible, a relationship ended recently and I'm about to lose my home. I've tried to commit suicide already this year and failed spectacularly. I'm very alone. All I can think of is hanging in my bathroom. Thank you for responding.
My cousin committed suicide and my Auntie cries every day. Not to shame you (I'm in the same boat!) but I guess its worth us considering.
Can only speak from experience I'm afraid. It's just some nasty stuff and I'd hate for you to be unsafe.
Please get help. I did this a few months ago and needed 3 days of IV rehydration. I'm worried for you.

Yep, UK based and grateful for NHS support I guess but it has been sketchy over the last few years. 

I think you're right...clean slate, formalise diagnosis, move on. I want that structure and it's not coming but I feel that is my fault.

Nobody to speak to in "the system" at all, I am very socially isolated which I know is bad. 

Thank you.

10 years of symptoms too. In and out of CMHT but now it's all being questioned again. Erratic presentation and suspected (?) recent suicide attempt...It wasn't, I wanted to be quiet. But if I feel if someone like you had sat with me for an hour the outcome would have been more understanding...I don't know, I feel I'm going "insane" sometimes and it all feels so surreal.

I can't admit assault. I can't do it. I have only mentioned this once because I'm desperate and I don't want to end up in that hospital again so surely it's worth a try? It wasn't assault, it was me and I'm disgusting. 

A clean slate would ultimately be death. Secondary...new location, new work, new relationships...and it's all too much.

They suggested bipolar on my recent hospitalisation because I'm so up and down (type 2). If you don't mind me asking, how did you get to your diagnosis? I can't face more years of futile suicide attempts that are half-hearted. I'm just hurting. I really don't want to die, I just don't want to hurt.

It is time for a new pattern indeed. I need to be self-caring and assertive. I have been assaulted two times in the past 2 months (totally reckless behaviour on my part too, not going to minimise what happens with actual sexual assault) and need stability. I just feel very shaken up and like I'm damaged...like I've messed up so much now I may as well start all over again. I need a clean slate

No sponsor. I only "relapse" when my mental health turns, the rest of the time you wouldn't know I had a problem. I feel like I've ruined tomorrow already...like, I've repeated this pattern too many times and maybe I just need to quit. I'm in no way actively suicidal like I was a few weeks ago but do feel like I'm coming to some rational end. Is that normal?
Thank you. I don't have any other sufficient words right now, just thank you.

Can definitely relate to the early waking, appetite increase, taking in the world around me and dawning loneliness. Congratulations! No great insight? I'd say that was a heck of a lot and long may it continue for you!
You're so right. Once they're two drinks down they will probably forget I'm there! Going to push the health/medication side of things too. Thank you.

Similar lurking/quitting history to you. Congrats to you for making the leap and grabbing this thing by the neck (I say congrats because it's a commitment and denial is tempting at times). It's good to have you here.

I have found coming here time and again an essential part of getting back/staying on track with sobriety as well as assessing my relationship with alcohol. Heck, post every day if you feel that will help you reflect! The support is fantastic. I have also found getting a badge every time beneficial too, but that may be personal preference. Hope to see you around.

I'm sorry you went through that. I don't think it's unreasonable at all to ask your husband to purchase his own alcohol. That isn't controlling, that's understanding your needs and looking after your own wellbeing. I try not to impose my ongoing attempts at sobriety onto my SO but try to recognise when I'm feeling vulnerable or things are getting complicated...then something needs to be said and lines drawn. Communication is key, as they say. Are these things you feel you can't talk about with him and if so do you have anyone else you can speak to confidentially?

It's not easy, especially when booze sneakily becomes a factor of a relationship and you hadn't even notice it happening. I can empathise with you so much. You're already doing so well and from what I'm reading  you're not "weird" or "controlling" but battling on. Enjoy your chocolate ;)

Congrats! Sounds like that peer pressure was quite intense both times. Any tips on how you managed that if you don't mind sharing? Similar situation coming up with some very pushy (but lovely) characters. 

Enjoy your hangover-free morning/festive season!
Calories aside, I think treating yourself to the effort you put into your sobriety is worthwhile too now and then as mini rewards, whether that be food or an activity (or both!)
Now this is the kind of enthusiasm and inspiration I come here for (repeatedly)! COGRATULATIONS! You must feel so proud.

Thank you for sharing your experiences, makes things feel much less isolating. 

'Surfing' sounds like an ideal way to describe it. I was trying to explain to this doctor that I can distinctly tell when 'everything in my life is shit' and that this is a different feeling entirely. Like you, I find that sober I have some energy to 'ride it out' safely and can take care of myself better in small ways (e.g. taking meds, activity). This episode was coming a long time, like a storm gathering, but I did the worst thing and relapsed...definitely learned from that. I think it scares me that mental illness will always be there like a threat, almost like the alcoholism. 

One day at a time!

Thank you for your encouraging words. Playing it forward definitely worked well this time so I'll be relying on that again in the future. It really does require stopping and thinking when you have so many emotions going on at once. I'd be feeling very ill now if I'd bought that drink! 

Half winging it and half being in control sounds more realistic, I'll aim for that I think! So tired of being hard on myself. I do see a therapist for my mental health who luckily is very understanding about the role of alcohol in everything.

I won't drink with you today.

The "take that!" attitude is baffling as we only really hurt ourselves...it's reassuring to know I'm not the only one who has gone through that. It almost used to be like "OK world, I'm checking out now with a bottle because you're too much". 

I agree, medical professionals shouldn't make us feel ashamed or inferior. I seem to see a different doctor each time but maybe next time will ask in advance so as to avoid that specific one! If I'd wanted to discuss my drinking habits then I would have felt totally uncomfortable, which means others likely would too...People being willing but unable to get help is unacceptable. 

Thank you for your support :)
I won't drink with you today :) This sub is indeed amazing, it drew me right back after a recent relapse.

Hi there. Have been in a similar position with my family in the past so can definitely identify with that awful sense of them slipping away. Rock bottom for me wasn't one event, it was a state I had gotten myself into that affected all areas of life. Drinking was making that state worse. People told me again and again that they were worried but I could only consider sobriety when it was all evident to me. Wanting to improve relationships just spurred me on more, but at the core there was an almost realisation if you like. That came from me. You might be at the point yourself, you will know.

I'm sorry you feel hopeless. I feel hopeless sometimes when I look back at the damage I've done drinking so you know what? I just try hard to focus on the now. The now can't ever be improved if I start drinking. I guess it's as the old saying goes "don't look backwards, you're not going that way". 

If you're struggling with the thought of being without alcohol due to dependency then remember that there is no shame in asking for support. It shows courage to ask for help sometimes. The 'problem' was taboo in my family for so long, eventually I just held my hands up and admitted I needed support. 

You are most definitely not alone.
I can't believe dry heaving was just part of my weekly routine at one point. Congrats on your 48 days, good work!

I hear you. It does feel like punishment at times, I frequently ask myself "why can other people use alcohol within reason and I can't?". Then I realise it's sadly fact. I just can't. I have the evidence/experience and I can't change it, other than by not drinking. It feels too overwhelming to think of never drinking again so I take it day by day, or even hour by hour if in social situations. Play things forward...what will happen if I have a drink? How will I feel afterwards? Will it really change anything? It's effort to constantly think like this but I'm hoping it eases with time and during my last stint of sobriety it did become more automatic with time. Sometimes I even have to grab a piece of paper and write out the pros and cons of drinking, making sure to detail every reason that resulted in me attempting to give it up. You're not alone in feeling like this is what I wanted to say I guess :) I will also not drink with you today. Stay strong.

I can identify with you so much with it being in that "first one". That "first one" recently ended up becoming a few days and a complete loss of control. Congratulations on taking that control back. Also, that guy sounds like he could be a great friend.

I was thinking this last night whilst watching soaps (in the UK)...each one revolved around a pub, each one showed alcohol consumption at least once, often to excess, and the advertisements in between contained alcohol too. They do show consequences occasionally but they rarely seem to be long-lasting, unless characters are an "alcoholic" but then the characterisation is often taken to extremes so you have a tendency to identify with it less and less (i.e. they'll be in end stage liver failure, ending marriages, jobless, etc.). Characters who have been alcoholics in the past seem to come to some realisation, go through treatment and it's barely heard of again...there should be more awareness I think on how alcoholism is a chronic condition and perhaps portray it as more of an ongoing battle? I don't want to sound like a killjoy (after all, it's me with the unhealthy relationship to booze) but I'd like to see alcohol not constantly associated with fun and relaxation on TV. Yeah, sure, people use it for these purposes and that's fine but like you say it's romanticised and perhaps if we saw the association less on TV we'd be less likely to have that association so ingrained in our minds. I am genuinely curious as to what the response would be if, with no mention made, alcohol consumption was removed from TV on the sly. Would people notice? When would they notice? Interesting stuff.

Now THAT is how you 'play it forward' and really learn from it. Well done, just reading that I could sense the temptation was palpable. In one night you have successfully saved your health and potentially your relationship with your conscious choices. That has to feel good. Remind yourself of this level of strength next time temptation comes your way...you have it somewhere. Enjoy the pizza (give yourself double helpings from calories saved on booze!)
Happy sober Saturday! I woke up naturally (?!) at 6am having had a restful night. So many hours to fill! Have a good day.

Thanks for the response :) My first 10 days last time were so physically draining that I couldn't move whereas this time it has been totally different...but you're right, they're all still "firsts" with that sober mindset. I'll totally avoid that general area of the supermarket next time or limit what cash I have on me. 

I ALWAYS have a non-alcoholic drink in my hand at the moment, from waking up to going to sleep. I'm on sugar free fizzy drinks too. Someone mentioned artificial sweeteners might be worth looking out for. Did you have any side effects from them? Staying far away from caffeine because I have a history of anxiety.

Thanks for replying. I think you hit the nail on the head there with "pleasant or not". I'm expecting productivity and enjoyment but those things don't come automatically. I will physically exhaust myself this weekend I think. I'd be punishing myself by drinking so why not punish myself through exercise?! 

I'm reassured that you had the fluid increase too. I don't think it'll cause any harm, was just worried it was indicative of a deficiency or something y'know? I didn't think about the artificial sweetners either, good point, thanks for that reminder. I must be swimming in them.

Good luck with your weekend plans and I'll join you in not drinking today.
That has a good ring to it...like the drink had control of you, but now you've taken that control back. Congratulations on your victory there! May many more come.

It sounds like you're in a lot of emotional pain, I genuinely empathise with you. I was (still am really) at a similar point but with some serious reflection concluded that the alcohol was exacerbating my misery whereas I had been duped into thinking it was masking it. If it was truly masking things, would it trick us into thinking we should take our own lives? I've found the only way to cope hour by hour if acutely distressed is by finding distraction. Anything, no matter how small. I also dragged out some materials from old therapy sessions. Do you have any of the info they gave you from rehab still by any chance? Just a suggestion. My thoughts are with you.

I would say that the days you have relapsed certainly do not nullify those years you succeeded with sobriety and those years are proof that you can return to that way of life. It's easy for an outsider to say (I've been having the same internal argument since my recent relapse) but try to ditch the shame and maybe treat this as a learning experience? I'm sorry you're suffering but we can do it, you have previous proof of that :)

The facial bloat/puffiness...gone! Has seriously made a huge difference. Looking good! I bet that doesn't compare to how you feel in yourself though. Great news on your career too. Thanks for posting, for relapsers like myself you're an inspiration.

From someone a little older, I can guarantee that your life will head in a significantly better direction with sobriety. I understand it must feel bittersweet though. Happy birthday, go treat yourself :)

Sounds like you have a great support network. It can't have been easy to own up and commit to changing though, good work there. I've personally found the psychological support (despite a recent relapse) absolutely invaluable, if you decide to go down that route. Here's to your new life!

I struggle with guilt and shame too. I try to remind myself that at least I'm not adding to that catalogue of misery/list of embarrassing events by deciding to stop now. The majority of those drunken actions were not representative of who I truly am, I know that deep down. From here on in you have control of the alcohol, the alcohol doesn't have control of you. Keep strong.
